The Letter Isn’t an Audit, and 30 Days Is the Window to Say So
 Vilma Rios Wed, October 21, 2026 at 4:00 PM CST 6 min read Quick Read 
 The IRS sent 1.6 million CP2000 letters last year, closing 987,460 cases and collecting $5.9 billion in additional assessments. 
 A broker reporting proceeds without cost basis can turn a $6,000 taxable gain into a $7,200 proposed bill, a problem fixed with just one brokerage statement. 
 Ignoring a CP2000 triggers a statutory notice of deficiency, leaving only 90 days to petition Tax Court before the IRS can assess and collect. 
 The biggest 401k decisions tend to get made once and never revisited: when to roll it over, what to hold inside it, and when to start taking money out. That is exactly what the report: 401k & IRA Tips and Answers was created to address, and it is free today. Read more here . (Sponsor) 
 The envelope from the IRS arrives in the fall, and page one shows a balance due big enough to need a comma. For many retirees, that's when panic sets in. A CP2000 letter means the IRS's records and your return disagree, and the law gives you the first chance to say which one is right. 
 Pheelings Media / iStock via Getty Images The IRS sent about 1.6 million of these "proposed changes" letters last year. Its own statistics show it closed 987,460 Automated Underreporter cases in fiscal 2025, which produced $5.9 billion in additional assessments. The response window printed on the letter is usually 30 days, or 60 days if you live outside the United States. 
 How a Computer Match Writes Your CP2000 Letter 
 The CP2000 comes from the IRS Automated Underreporter program. The program checks every W-2 and 1099 that payers file against the numbers on your return. A Treasury Inspector General for Tax Administration report found it routinely flags more than 20 million individual returns with discrepancies each year.

 The IRS describes the letter as a proposal to adjust your income, payments, credits, and/or deductions. It comes from a computer match, and no auditor is assigned. Under section § 7522(b)(2), any notice "generated out of any information return matching program" has to explain its basis, so the letter names the exact form behind the change. 
 Story Continues Common triggers include forgotten Forms 1099s and stock or crypto sales without basis. Sometimes the taxpayer never saw the triggering form. It went to an old address after a move, sat unopened in a brokerage's online document center, or showed up as a corrected form after the return was filed. 
 A $40,000 Stock Sale Turns Into a $7,200 Proposed Bill 
 Consider a sample case: a retired couple in their late 60s who file jointly for 2024. Their other income puts their long-term gains in the 15% capital gains bracket. They sold an old stock holding for $40,000 and had paid $34,000 for it. Their broker had switched them to paperless statements, the 1099-B sat unopened online, and the sale never made it onto their return. 
 The broker reported the proceeds without the cost basis, so the matching program had nothing to subtract. It taxed the whole $40,000. A CP2000 can also propose the accuracy-related penalty, which equals 20% of the underpayment under 26 U.S.C. § 6662(a).

 With the basis documented, the couple's bill falls from $7,200 to about $900 plus interest. That's a gap of $6,300, and closing it takes one brokerage statement. 
 Your 30-Day Window: Agree, Disagree, or Fix the Form 1099 
 Identify the form. Check the payer and amount the letter lists against a wage and income transcript, which you can request on Form 4506-T or view in your IRS online account. 
 If you agree, sign the response form and pay. When full payment isn't possible, request a payment plan on Form 9465. 
 If you disagree, the IRS tells you to state whether you agree or disagree with the notice and include any supporting documentation. Our couple would send trade confirmations showing their $34,000 basis. 
 If the Form 1099 is wrong, contact the company that issued it. IRS guidance says the agency can't correct an incorrect Form 1099-K, and a corrected Form 1099-R replaces the corresponding original. 
 Silence Turns a Proposal Into a Tax Court Deadline 
 Without a response, the IRS treats your silence as agreement. It finalizes the proposed changes and sends a statutory notice of deficiency by certified or registered mail under 26 U.S.C. § 6212(a). From that mailing date, you have 90 days, or 150 days if the notice goes to someone outside the United States, to petition the Tax Court. After that window closes, the IRS can assess the tax and start collecting. 
 Late letters come with one break. If you filed on time and the IRS didn't send a notice saying your liability within the 36-month period that starts on the later of your filing date or the return's due date, interest and certain penalties may be suspended for a limited period. 
 Expect slow replies. The IRS lost approximately 27% of its Examination and Collection staff from fiscal 2024 to fiscal 2025, according to the inspector general. Mail your response by certified mail, keep the receipt, and keep a full copy of everything you send. 
 One costly mistake is paying the proposed amount without checking it, especially when the trigger is a stock sale with no reported basis. If the letter involves several years or a large sum, it's worth having a CPA, an enrolled agent or a credential tax professional check the math before the deadline printed on page one.
